transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

I’m here because… I don’t know, it’s gotten to the point where I can’t really function normally around people the way I used to. I keep seeing this droop, this unevenness around my mouth and my jaw—especially in photos, but also in mirrors, windows, even on my phone screen when it goes dark. It feels like it’s the first thing anyone would notice.

People tell me I look fine, or that they don’t see what I’m talking about, but that almost makes it worse because I feel like they’re just being polite. To me it’s very obvious. Like one side is lower or heavier, and then my whole face looks wrong.

And it’s starting to affect work. I’m an architect, so I have to meet with clients and give presentations, and I’ve started avoiding them when I can. I’ll make excuses or try to have someone else speak, because I can’t stop thinking they’re staring at my mouth or jaw instead of listening to me. So… that’s why I came in. It’s taking over more than I want to admit.
Do you ever think that maybe your mouth and jaw actually look normal, and it's just your perception of them that's off?

I mean… logically, I suppose I can understand that maybe other people don’t see it the way I do. They tell me I look fine, they say my mouth and jaw look normal, or that I’m exaggerating it. But when I look—especially in a photo, or even just a reflection in a window—it doesn’t feel like a question. It feels obvious. Like one side is drooping or heavier, and then I can’t see anything else.

So yes, there’s a small part of me that wonders if my perception is somehow… off, because otherwise why would everyone keep saying they don’t notice it? But that thought doesn’t really stick. The moment I see my face again, it’s right there, and I feel embarrassed, almost exposed. It’s gotten to where I avoid presentations or meeting clients if I can, because I’m sure they’re looking at my mouth and jaw instead of listening to what I’m saying.
Do you think it's possible that your mouth and jaw actually are uneven, even if other people don't see it that way?

Yes… yes, I do think it’s possible. Honestly, most of the time I think it’s more than possible — it feels like it’s just true. I know people say they don’t see it, or they say, “No, your face looks fine,” but when I look at myself, especially in photos or any kind of reflection, I can’t stop seeing that droop around my mouth and jaw. One side just looks heavier or lower to me, and once I notice it, it’s all I can focus on.

It’s not like I’m looking for something tiny on purpose. It just jumps out at me. And then I start thinking, well, maybe other people are just being kind, or maybe they don’t want to embarrass me by admitting it. Because to me it feels so obvious that I don’t understand how they wouldn’t see it.

And it’s gotten bad enough that I’ve started avoiding presentations and clients when I can, because I’m sitting there imagining they’re looking at my mouth instead of listening to what I’m saying. So even if other people say they don’t notice it, I still feel like the unevenness is there.
Do you think there's any chance at all that you might be mistaken about the unevenness of your mouth and jaw?

I mean… there’s maybe a tiny chance, yes. I can say that because I’m sitting here and I know people keep telling me they don’t see it. They’ll say my mouth looks normal, or my jaw isn’t uneven, and I understand that, logically, that should mean something.

But when I actually see myself — in a photo, or a reflection, or even just my phone screen when it goes dark — it’s like all of that disappears. I can’t stop seeing this droop around my mouth and jaw. It looks so obvious to me, like one side is lower or heavier, and then I can’t look at my face as a whole anymore. That one thing takes over.

So I suppose I might be mistaken in the sense that other people don’t seem to react to it the way I do. But it doesn’t feel like I’m mistaken. It feels real enough that I’ve started avoiding presentations and clients, because I’m worried they’re noticing it too and just not saying anything.
Does your perception of the unevenness around your mouth and jaw ever change, or does it always look the same to you?

It changes a bit, yes, but not in a reassuring way. I mean, it’s always there to me — that’s the problem. I can’t really remember the last time I looked at a photo or caught my reflection and didn’t immediately go to my mouth and jaw. But some moments it looks… worse, I guess. Like in certain lighting, or in a photo taken from the wrong angle, it looks like the droop is much more obvious, like one side of my mouth is pulling down or my jaw is sitting unevenly.

And then other times it might look slightly less severe, but I still see it. It doesn’t disappear. Even if someone says, “You look fine,” I’ll look again and think, no, it’s right there, how can they not see that? So it isn’t that one day I think I look normal and the next day I don’t. It’s more like the intensity changes, but the unevenness is always the first thing I notice.

That’s part of why I’m here, honestly. I feel like I can’t stop seeing it in every photo and reflection, and it’s gotten to where I’m avoiding presentations and clients because I’m afraid they’re focused on my mouth and jaw too.
Do you think anyone else actually sees the unevenness you're describing, or do you believe they're just not telling you?

I think… I think they probably do see it, at least some of them. Or maybe they see something and just don’t want to say it. That’s the part I get stuck on, because when people tell me I look fine, I don’t really feel reassured. I know they may mean it kindly, but in my head I’m thinking, they’re just trying not to hurt my feelings, or they noticed and decided it would be rude to mention.

Because to me it’s so obvious. Every photo, every reflection, I go straight to that area around my mouth and jaw — that droop, the unevenness. I can’t just look at my whole face normally anymore. It’s like my eyes lock onto it immediately, and then I start imagining that everyone else’s eyes are going there too.

That’s why it’s affected work so much. I’m an architect, I’m supposed to be able to speak to clients and do presentations, and instead I’m worrying that they’re staring at my mouth when I talk, or noticing one side of my jaw looks lower. So yes, when they say they don’t see it, part of me thinks they’re just not telling me. I’m here because I can’t seem to get past that feeling.
Has there ever been a time when you didn't notice the unevenness around your mouth and jaw?

Honestly… not really, not anymore. I mean, I’m sure there must have been a time before I was so focused on it, because I didn’t always live like this, checking every photo and reflection. But lately, I can’t remember looking at myself without immediately going to that area — my mouth, my jaw, that droop or unevenness.

Even if it’s just a quick reflection in a window or my phone screen when it’s dark, my eyes go straight there. And in photos it’s worse, because then I can zoom in or stare at it, and it feels so obvious that I don’t understand how other people can say they don’t see anything. I know they tell me I look fine, but it doesn’t land that way for me.

So if you mean recently, no — I don’t think there’s really a time when I don’t notice it. It’s like it’s always the first thing I see, and it’s gotten to the point where I avoid presentations and clients because I’m worried they’re seeing exactly what I’m seeing.
Do you think it's possible that your perception of the unevenness is not based in reality?

I mean… I know that’s what you’re asking me to consider, and part of me understands why you’d ask it. But it’s very hard for me to believe it’s not based in reality, because when I look at myself it feels so obvious. I see this droop, this unevenness around my mouth and jaw, and my eyes go straight to it every single time.

It’s not like I’m looking for something vague and then convincing myself. It feels like it’s right there in every photo, every reflection, even when I catch myself quickly in a window or on my phone screen. And when people say I look fine, I want to believe them, but I don’t really feel convinced. I start thinking maybe they’re being polite, or maybe they don’t want to embarrass me.

So… possible? I suppose I can say it’s possible because I’m here, and because this has gotten out of hand. I’ve started avoiding presentations and clients because I’m so worried they’re seeing my mouth and jaw the way I see them. But emotionally, no, it doesn’t feel unreal to me. It feels painfully real.
Do you think there's any situation or proof that could convince you that the unevenness around your mouth and jaw isn't actually there?

I don’t know. I wish I could say yes, because that would mean there’s some way out of this, but when I imagine it, I’m not sure what would actually convince me.

People have told me I look fine. They’ve said they don’t notice anything, or that my face looks normal, and for a few seconds maybe I try to take that in. But then I’ll see myself in a photo or catch my reflection somewhere, and immediately I’m back to seeing the droop around my mouth, the unevenness in my jaw. It’s like whatever reassurance I got just disappears.

Maybe if there were some kind of objective measurement or something, I’d want to believe it. But even then, I’m afraid I’d think, well, maybe the lighting was different, or maybe they measured the wrong thing, or maybe it only shows when I’m talking. That’s how stuck I feel with it.

I’m here because I really can’t stop seeing it. Every photo, every reflection, that’s where my eyes go first. And it feels so obvious to me that even when other people say I look fine, I still end up avoiding presentations and clients because I’m convinced they’re going to notice my mouth and jaw the way I do. So… I want there to be proof that would help, but right now I honestly don’t know what would be strong enough.
Do you ever find yourself unable to stop thinking about the unevenness of your mouth and jaw, even when you're trying to focus on something else?

Yes. Constantly, honestly. Even when I’m trying to focus on work or listen to someone, part of my mind is still on my mouth and jaw — like, how it looks, whether the droop is showing, whether the unevenness is obvious from whatever angle they’re seeing me.

It’s worst with photos and reflections, because once I see it, I can’t unsee it. My eyes go straight there every time, and then it kind of stays with me afterward. Even if someone tells me I look fine, I keep replaying it in my head and thinking, “No, it’s there, it’s obvious.” It feels like I’m fighting with what they’re saying versus what I’m seeing.

And it’s gotten to where it interferes with things I should be able to just do. Presentations, clients — I avoid them when I can, because I’m so preoccupied with the idea that they’ll be looking at that part of my face instead of listening to me. I know that probably sounds excessive, but in the moment it feels impossible to put it aside.
Is your concern about your mouth and jaw the only thing you worry about when it comes to your appearance, or are there other aspects of how you look that also bother you?

It’s mostly — really, almost entirely — the mouth and jaw. That’s the thing I can’t get away from. I don’t sit there cataloging every part of my face or body in the same way. It’s this droop, this unevenness around my mouth and jaw, that just pulls my attention over and over.

Like, I can look at a photo and maybe someone else would see the whole picture, but I don’t. My eyes go straight to that area. Same with reflections — bathroom mirror, car window, phone screen, anything. I immediately check whether one side looks lower or whether my jaw looks off. And then once I see it, I feel like it’s all anyone else could possibly see too.

People tell me I look fine, and I know I’ve said that, but it doesn’t really settle it for me. It might calm me down for a moment, but then I see myself again and it feels obvious all over again. That’s why I’m here, really. It’s not that I have a long list of appearance things I’m equally worried about — it’s that this one thing has taken over so much that I’ve started avoiding presentations and meeting with clients because I’m convinced they’ll notice my mouth and jaw instead of listening to what I’m saying.
Do you think your perception of the unevenness could be considered an unreasonable or unrealistic concern by others?

I suppose… yes, I can see that other people might think it’s unreasonable or unrealistic. I mean, people have told me over and over that I look fine, that they don’t see what I’m talking about, or that it’s not noticeable. So I understand, in a logical way, that they might look at me and think I’m making too much of it.

But it doesn’t feel unrealistic to me when I see it. That’s the problem. In every photo, every reflection, my eyes go straight to my mouth and jaw, and I see this droop, this unevenness, like one side isn’t sitting right. And once I see it, it feels so obvious that I can’t really believe other people aren’t seeing it too.

So yes, I can imagine someone else saying, “This isn’t as bad as you think,” or “You’re focused on something minor,” but inside it doesn’t feel minor at all. It feels like it’s right there on my face, and it’s gotten to the point where I’ve avoided presentations and clients because I’m worried they’ll be looking at that instead of listening to me. So… I know others may think my concern is excessive, but I still can’t stop seeing it.
Has your concern about the unevenness of your mouth and jaw ever gone away for a while, even if it came back later?

Not really, no. I mean… I wish I could say it goes away for stretches, but it doesn’t feel like it does. It may quiet down for a little while if I’m completely distracted, but then I’ll catch myself in a reflection or see a photo and my eyes go straight back to my mouth and jaw.

That’s really why I’m here — because I can’t stop seeing this droop, this unevenness around my mouth and jaw. Every photo, every reflection, it’s like that’s the only thing I can focus on. And even when people tell me I look fine, or they say they don’t notice anything, it doesn’t last. For a moment I might try to believe them, but then I see myself again and it feels obvious all over again.

So no, I wouldn’t say it has really gone away. It’s become this constant thing in the background, and sometimes very much in the foreground, to the point where I’ve started avoiding presentations and clients because I’m so worried they’ll be looking at that instead of listening to me.
Has there ever been a period of time when you didn't think about the unevenness of your mouth and jaw at all?

No… I don’t think there’s been a time when I didn’t think about it at all. Maybe if I’m really absorbed in something for a short while, I’m not actively thinking, “my mouth, my jaw,” every second. But it’s never gone in the way you’re asking, like some period where I just forgot about it or looked normal to myself.

It’s always there waiting, if that makes sense. I’ll see myself in a photo or even just catch a reflection in a window, and immediately my attention goes straight to that droop, that unevenness around my mouth and jaw. And then it’s like the whole rest of my face disappears. I can’t see what other people say they see.

Even when people tell me I look fine, I can hear the words, and maybe I try to accept it for a moment, but it doesn’t really take. Because as soon as I see myself again, it feels obvious all over again. That’s why it’s become so hard with work things, like presentations or meeting clients. I start thinking they’re going to be focused on my mouth and jaw instead of what I’m saying. So no, I can’t really say there’s been a period where I didn’t think about it at all.
Has your concern about the unevenness of your mouth and jaw affected your relationships with friends or family, in addition to your work?

Yes… it has. I think at first I wanted to tell myself it was mostly a work problem, because work is where I have to be seen and judged and stand in front of people. But it’s not staying contained there anymore.

With my family, I’ve started missing things or arriving late or making excuses because I just can’t face being looked at. Family gatherings that used to be normal now feel like this whole ordeal, like I have to prepare myself to be seen from different angles or photographed. And then I feel terrible, because it’s not that I don’t care about them. I do. But I get so caught up in how my mouth and jaw look that I either don’t go, or I’m there but not really present.

And with friends, it’s similar. I’ve been avoiding networking events too, especially since there have been some award-related things I should be attending. Those are important for my career, but they’re also social, and I’ve been missing them because I can’t stand the idea of people seeing my face up close or taking pictures. I know that sounds extreme, but in the moment it feels impossible.

It’s gotten bad enough that I cancelled a major client presentation at the last minute. I just couldn’t make myself go in front of the room. And then of course everything spirals from there — project deadlines start slipping, people are disappointed or confused, and at home my family is upset because I’m withdrawing or ruining plans. It feels like things are starting to fall apart around this, honestly. Not just work, but relationships too.
Do you think it's possible that your perception of the unevenness is a result of your own mind playing a trick on you, rather than an actual physical flaw?

I mean… I understand why you’re asking that. Part of me knows people keep telling me they don’t see what I’m seeing, or that it’s not noticeable, and I try to take that in. I really do. But then I see a photo of myself, or I catch my reflection somewhere, and it’s like my eyes go straight to my mouth and jaw, and I can’t unsee it.

So I guess… maybe it’s possible my mind is making it bigger than it is? I don’t know. But it doesn’t feel like a trick when I’m looking at it. It feels completely obvious to me, like there’s this droop or unevenness around my mouth and jaw, and I don’t understand how other people aren’t seeing it the way I do.

That’s why it’s been so hard with presentations and clients. I’ll be trying to focus on what I’m supposed to say, but in my head I’m thinking they’re looking at my mouth, noticing the unevenness, judging it. Even if someone reassures me beforehand, the second I see myself again, it all comes back. So… I can say maybe there’s a chance my perception is off, but emotionally it feels very real.
Do you think it's possible that the unevenness you see is something that only you can see, and not something that actually exists?

I… I suppose I have to admit it’s possible, because people keep telling me they don’t see it the way I do. I hear that, and I’m not trying to be difficult. But when I look at myself, especially in photos or in a reflection, it doesn’t feel like something only I can see. It feels right there, like this droop or unevenness around my mouth and jaw is the first thing anyone would notice.

That’s really why I’m here. I can’t stop seeing it. I’ll be fine for maybe a moment, and then I catch my face in a window or someone takes a picture, and all I can focus on is my mouth and jaw. Even if someone says, “You look fine,” it doesn’t settle in me, because to me it looks so obvious.

And it’s gotten to where I’m avoiding things because of it — presentations, meeting clients, situations where people are looking at me closely. I keep thinking they’re going to notice the unevenness instead of listening to what I’m saying. So… yes, maybe in a logical sense it could be something only I’m seeing, but it doesn’t feel that way at all. It feels very real when I see myself.
Do you think it's possible that the unevenness you perceive is not something that can be measured or proven to exist objectively?

I guess… yes, maybe it’s possible that it’s not something you could measure in some objective way. I don’t know. That’s hard for me to say, because when I see it, it doesn’t feel vague or imagined. It feels like this very obvious droop and unevenness around my mouth and jaw, like my face just isn’t sitting right.

But I’m here because I can’t stop seeing it. In every photo, every reflection, it’s the first thing my eyes go to. And even when people tell me I look fine, or that they don’t notice anything, it doesn’t really change what I see. I might believe them for a second, or try to, but then I see myself again and it just comes rushing back.

So… maybe if someone tried to measure it, they wouldn’t find what I’m seeing. Maybe it wouldn’t prove anything. But to me it feels so obvious that I’ve started avoiding presentations and clients, because I feel like they’re going to be looking at my mouth instead of listening to me. It’s like I know there’s this question of whether it can be proven, but emotionally I’m already reacting as if it’s absolutely there.
Do you think that if multiple doctors and experts examined your face, they would all agree that there is no noticeable unevenness around your mouth and jaw?

I don’t know… I mean, maybe they would. If several doctors looked at me and all said there was no noticeable unevenness, I suppose I’d have to hear that. I’m not saying I know more than experts. But the problem is, I’m here because I can’t stop seeing it myself.

It’s this droop, or unevenness, around my mouth and jaw — especially in photos or when I catch my reflection unexpectedly. My eyes just go straight there, every single time. And even if someone tells me I look fine, or says they don’t see anything, it doesn’t really stay with me. For a moment I might think, “Okay, maybe it’s not as bad as I think,” but then I see myself again and it feels completely obvious.

So if doctors said they didn’t notice it, part of me would want to believe them, but another part of me would still be thinking, “How can they not see it?” That’s what’s made it so hard at work too. I’ve started avoiding presentations and client meetings because I feel like people are going to be staring at my mouth and jaw instead of listening to me. So… logically, yes, maybe experts would agree it’s not noticeable, but emotionally it doesn’t feel that way at all.
Do you think you would still see the unevenness if you couldn't see any reflections or photos of yourself for an extended period?

I think… if I couldn’t see reflections or photos for a while, maybe I wouldn’t have that same immediate jolt of seeing it right in front of me. Because that’s what sets it off the worst — a photo, a mirror, a window, even a dark screen sometimes. My eyes go straight to my mouth and jaw, and then I’m just stuck on it.

But I don’t think it would completely go away in my mind. I’d probably still be thinking about it, wondering how my face looked while I was talking, imagining that droop or unevenness even if I couldn’t check it. Because I’m here because I can’t stop seeing it when I do see myself, and it feels so obvious to me. Even when people tell me I look fine, it doesn’t really erase it.

So maybe without mirrors or photos I’d get a little less triggered moment to moment, but I think I’d still be preoccupied with it. I’d still be worrying that other people could see it, especially if I had to give a presentation or meet with clients. That’s part of why I’ve started avoiding those situations — I feel like they’re going to be looking at my mouth and jaw instead of listening to what I’m saying.
